newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. Vice President Gore plays up ties with Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Vice President Gore plays up ties with Japan.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Tokyo at the start of his eight-day Asian trip and immediately underscored the importance of ties with Japan.
"Although the journey can seem to be a long one, I'm conscious immediately upon arrival of how close we are," Gore said at Tokyo's Haneda airport after stepping down from his Air Force Two plane.
"Indeed there is no more important bilateral relationship than that between the United States and Japan."
Gore said his visit was intended to reaffirm U.S. commitment to the region.
"The security and prosperity of the United States is vitally tied to the Asia-Pacific region and to our partnership and friendship with Japan."
Gore was to hold talks with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda over dinner later on Sunday and then meet Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday before leaving for Beijing.
In talks with Ikeda and Hashimoto, Gore was expected to exchange views on the China policies of the two countries after the death of paramount Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping.
Japanese leaders were expected to reaffirm Tokyo's plan to keep U.S. bases on southern Japan's Okinawa island, the nation's biggest domestic political problem.

Japanese government leases on 3,000 plots of private land on U.S. bases expire in May and Hashimoto said on Sunday he may try to push through parliament a special law to bypass a lengthy land expropriation process.
Okinawa is home to more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan, a legacy of the post-World War Two U.S. military occupation that ended in 1972.
In Beijing, Gore was expected to tackle thorny issues with Chinese leaders including allegations that China tried to illegally influence the outcome of last year's U.S. elections.
Gore flies to South Korea on Friday for negotiations on prospects of North Korea's participation in proposed four-way peace talks on the Korean Peninsula.
The talks among the two Koreas, China and the United States are designed to replace a 1950-1953 Korean War armistice with a peace treaty.
